summary: A white paper summarizing factors in judging whether an IPng proposal could succeed in the marketplace. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This white paper argues that a new Internet protocol must offer a clear benefit to gain adoption. It examines new features, costs, and connectivity as possible reasons to move from IPv4 to IPng.

questions: what would make ipng viable in the marketplace
why might ipv4 users migrate to ipng
subtitle: A 1994 analysis of market viability as a criterion for IPng proposals.

tldr.problem: An IPng proposal would have to compete with the established IPv4 base, and network operators would need a reason to take on migration effort and cost.
tldr.mechanism: The memo considers three possible migration drivers: new functionality, lower costs, or connectivity to hosts otherwise unreachable through IPv4.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that IPng would need clearly improved functionality and some form of transparent access between IPv4 and IPng communities to be viable in the marketplace.

today: RFC 1669 is Informational and records a 1994 analysis of market viability for IPng proposals. It does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Market Viability as a Requirement
sections.content:
The memo argues that adoption in an open marketplace depends on customer demand and perceived benefit. Because deploying internetworking technology can require substantial effort, a candidate IPng technology must offer a return that justifies the work.

Bundling a protocol with computer systems may help promote it, but the RFC says that this alone cannot ensure acceptance against a mature IPv4 base.
sections.plainLanguage: Organizations need a reason to adopt a new protocol. The memo says promotion alone is not enough when IPv4 is already established.

sections.title: Possible Reasons to Migrate
sections.content:
The memo identifies three possible reasons for existing IPv4 users to migrate: functionality not found in IPv4, reduced costs, or connectivity to hosts otherwise unreachable via IPv4. It says migration would add training and engineering costs, making cost savings unlikely as a reason by itself.

It argues that existing IPv4 sites would see little direct connectivity benefit until IPv4 address assignments were no longer available and IPng-only sites appeared.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper considers new capabilities, lower costs, and access to otherwise unreachable systems as possible reasons to switch. It argues that the case for switching may be weak before IPv4 addresses run out.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPng Connectivity
sections.content:
The RFC says the IPng proposals then under consideration could not provide complete connectivity between IPv4-only and IPng-only sites, because not all IPng addresses could be mapped into IPv4 space. It notes that the proposals did not then call for dynamic network address translation and considers that address-translation devices and services were likely to develop.

Its conclusion is that IPng needs clearly improved functionality and some form of transparent access between the IPv4 and IPng communities after IPv4 address depletion.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo warns that IPv4-only and IPng-only networks might not reach every system in the other group. It says a viable proposal needs both better capabilities and a way to bridge the two communities.

references.text: Gross, P., ed., "Internet Next Generation Architecture", RFC 1550, December 1993.
